topics.title: What is a group? Features, and how groups differ from crowds, teams and audiences

learn.hook: Forty people waiting at a bus stop and eleven players in the Indian cricket team — both are 'people together'. But only one is a true group. What's the difference?
points: Groups influence how we think and act. (In the rationalised syllabus this chapter covers the nature and formation of groups, types of groups, and group influences such as social loafing and group polarisation.)

A group is an organised system of two or more individuals who interact and are interdependent, have common motives, have set role relationships among members, and have norms that regulate members' behaviour.

Features: a social unit of two or more people who see themselves as belonging to the group; common motives and goals; interdependence (one member's actions affect others); members trying to satisfy needs through joint association and influencing each other; interaction governed by a set of norms; and defined roles.

A crowd is a collection of people present at a place by chance, with no structure, no feeling of belongingness and no interdependence; crowd behaviour can be irrational. An audience is a collection of people gathered for a special purpose, such as a film or a cricket match; it is generally passive, but may sometimes turn into a mob.

A team is a special kind of group whose members have complementary skills and are committed to a common goal, for which they hold themselves mutually accountable. In groups, performance depends on individual contributions; in teams, both individual contributions and teamwork matter, producing positive synergy.

example.q: Classify: (a) people gathered after a minor road accident, (b) a school's quiz team with a history expert, a science expert and a sports expert, (c) viewers at a cinema hall.
steps: (a) Gathered by chance, no structure → crowd.
(b) Complementary skills, common goal, mutual accountability → team.
(c) Gathered for a special purpose, mostly passive → audience.

learn.reallife: An ISRO mission team brings together engineers with complementary skills — propulsion, software, navigation — all accountable for one launch. That's a team, not just a group.

topics.title: Why people join groups and how groups form

learn.hook: Why do you join a WhatsApp group of classmates, a dance club or a coaching batch? Each one fills a need — and some are formed simply because you sit close together.
points: Security: being in a group reduces insecurity and gives comfort and protection. Status: membership of a recognised group gives a feeling of importance, power and status.
Self-esteem: groups give feelings of self-worth and a positive social identity. Satisfaction of psychological and social needs: belongingness, giving and receiving attention, love and power.
Goal achievement: groups help achieve goals that cannot be achieved alone. Knowledge and information: groups provide information and widen our knowledge.

Group formation factors: proximity (repeated interaction with people nearby, such as classmates or neighbours), similarity (people like those with similar interests and attitudes; similarity also validates our views) and common motives and goals.

example.q: Ananya joins her college's robotics club because (a) she wants to build a robot for a national contest, (b) club members are known as the 'tech elite' on campus, and (c) she can learn from seniors. Name the reasons.
steps: (a) Achieving a goal not possible alone → goal achievement.
(b) Being part of a recognised, admired group → status.
(c) Learning from others → knowledge and information.
example.answer: (a) Goal achievement, (b) Status, (c) Knowledge and information.

learn.reallife: Hostel friendships in Indian colleges often start simply because students live on the same floor — proximity at work.

topics.title: Stages of group formation and group structure

learn.hook: A new project team: first awkward introductions, then arguments over who does what, then a rhythm sets in — and finally they deliver. Tuckman mapped this journey.
points: Bruce Tuckman's stages: Forming — uncertainty about the group, its goal and how to achieve it; members get to know each other; excitement and apprehension. Storming — intragroup conflict over how to achieve the goal, who controls the group and resources, and who does which task; at the end, a hierarchy of leadership develops.

Norming — members develop norms about group behaviour, leading to a positive group identity. Performing — the group's structure has evolved and is accepted, and the group works towards its goal (the final stage for some groups).

Adjourning — once the purpose is achieved, the group may be disbanded (e.g., a committee formed for a school function). Groups do not always move through the stages in a fixed order; they may go back and forth.

Group structure develops as members interact: roles (socially defined expectations people are expected to fulfil), norms (expected standards of behaviour and beliefs, agreed and enforced by members — the group's unwritten rules), status (the relative social position given to members; it may be ascribed, as through seniority, or achieved, through expertise or hard work) and cohesiveness (togetherness and mutual attraction among members — the 'we-feeling').

example.q: Map a school annual-day committee to Tuckman's stages: (1) members meet and feel unsure, (2) they argue over who will host, (3) they agree on rules for rehearsals, (4) they put on the show, (5) the committee is dissolved.
steps: (1) Forming
(2) Storming
(3) Norming
(4) Performing
(5) Adjourning

learn.reallife: IPL franchise squads assembled through auctions go through forming and storming in pre-season camps; the best ones reach norming and performing quickly.

learn.hook: Your family, your school's NCC unit, your lunch-break gang and the rival school's team. Each is a different type of group — and each affects you differently.
points: Primary groups are pre-existing formations usually given to the individual (such as the family). They involve face-to-face interaction, close physical proximity and warm emotional bonds, are central to individual functioning, shape values and ideals, and have less permeable boundaries.

Secondary groups are joined by choice (such as a professional association or a hobby club). Relationships are more impersonal, indirect and less frequent, and it is easy to leave and join another group.

Formal groups have explicitly stated functions, roles and rules (such as an office, a university or a school council). Informal groups form without specific rules, and members have close relationships (such as a group of friends).

Ingroup refers to one's own group ('we'); outgroup refers to another group ('they'). Ingroup members are seen as similar and are viewed favourably; outgroup members are often seen differently and less favourably.

Other collectivities include crowds (chance gatherings), audiences (gathered for a purpose, generally passive) and mobs (with a definite sense of purpose, polarised attention, homogeneity of thought and behaviour, and impulsivity).

example.q: Classify the group types: (a) Rohit's family, (b) the Bar Council he joins as a lawyer, (c) his group of college friends, (d) his company's HR department.
steps: (a) Given, warm, face-to-face → primary (and informal).
(b) Joined by choice, impersonal → secondary (and formal).
(c) No set rules, close bonds → informal.
(d) Explicit rules and roles → formal.

learn.reallife: When two IPL franchises clash, fans strongly feel 'us' versus 'them' — a vivid example of ingroup and outgroup feelings, which is healthiest when the rivalry stays friendly and respectful.

learn.hook: In tug-of-war, does each extra person pull as hard as they would alone? Experiments say no — and the reason has a name: social loafing.
points: Social facilitation: performance on well-learned or simple tasks improves in the presence of others (Norman Triplett found cyclists rode faster when racing with others than alone). The presence of others raises arousal; for new or complex tasks, performance may instead suffer.

Social loafing is a reduction in individual effort when working on a collective task, in which outputs are pooled with those of other members (e.g., tug-of-war). Latané and colleagues found people clapped and cheered less loudly per person in groups than alone.

Reasons: members feel less responsible for the overall task; motivation decreases because individual contributions are not evaluated; the group's performance is not compared with other groups; there is improper or no coordination; and belonging to the group is not important to members — it is only an aggregate of individuals. (Responsibility is spread or diffused across members.)

Reducing social loafing: make each person's effort identifiable; increase pressure to work hard by making members committed to successful performance; increase the apparent importance or value of the task; make people feel their individual contribution is important; and strengthen group cohesiveness.

example.q: In a group project, only Riya does most of the work while others contribute little. Suggest two ways the teacher can reduce social loafing.
steps: Assign each member a specific, named part so individual effort is identifiable.
Make the project important (e.g., a public presentation) and build cohesiveness so members care about the outcome.
example.answer: Make individual efforts identifiable and increase task importance and group cohesiveness.

learn.reallife: In big office meetings in Indian companies, people often stay quiet expecting 'someone else will speak up'. Assigning named action points reduces that loafing.

Answer: Produced less noise per person than when alone

quiz.q: Case: A cleanliness drive in a housing society has 50 volunteers, but many just stand around chatting. The organiser then gives each volunteer a named stretch of road to clean. Why will this help?
options: It makes individual effort identifiable, reducing social loafing
quiz.explain: When each person's work is identifiable, loafing drops.
steps: A named stretch of road for each volunteer makes individual effort identifiable.
That reduces social loafing.
Answer: It makes individual effort identifiable, reducing social loafing
quiz.mistake: Thinks assigning areas spreads responsibility further.

teach.ask: Gappu complains: 'When ten of us carry a branch, I don't push as hard. Why? And how can we fix it?'
teach.praise: Oops, that's social loafing! Make each bird's effort identifiable and make the task matter. Heave-ho!
teach.nudge: How can we make sure every bird pulls its weight?

revise.summary: Social facilitation is better performance on simple or well-learned tasks in others' presence (Triplett). Social loafing is reduced individual effort on pooled group tasks (Latané), caused by low responsibility and evaluation, and reduced by identifiability, importance and cohesiveness.
remember: Latané: less clapping per person in groups
Reduce loafing: identifiable effort, commitment, task importance, individual contribution, cohesiveness
traps: Others' presence does not always improve performance: complex new tasks may suffer

learn.hook: Each member of a committee mildly favours a new flyover. After an hour of discussion, the group votes to build it immediately, whatever the cost. How did 'mild' become 'extreme'?
points: Group polarisation: groups are more likely to take extreme decisions than individuals alone; the group's initial position becomes stronger after discussion.

Reasons: (1) in the company of like-minded people, members hear new arguments favouring their own viewpoint; (2) when others share the same view, members feel their view is validated by the public — a bandwagon effect; (3) members perceive like-minded others as an ingroup, identify with the group and conform, so views become strengthened.

Groupthink (Irving Janis) is a related, extreme outcome of highly cohesive groups: the desire for consensus overrides realistic evaluation of alternatives. Signs include an illusion of unanimity, self-censorship of doubts and pressure on dissenters, often leading to poor decisions.
Preventing poor group decisions: encourage critical evaluation, invite outside opinions, and assign someone to play 'devil's advocate'.

example.q: Before discussion, each member of a school council mildly supports banning phones on campus. After discussion they vote for a total ban with heavy fines. Explain using the reasons for group polarisation.
steps: Members heard new arguments supporting the ban (more reasons to agree).
Seeing others agree validated their view (bandwagon effect).
Identifying with the like-minded group led them to conform and strengthen the position.
example.answer: Exposure to new supporting arguments, bandwagon validation and ingroup identification made the decision more extreme.

learn.reallife: Social media echo chambers in India and elsewhere show group polarisation online: like-minded users share supporting posts, and views grow more extreme over time.

Agreement validates views (bandwagon effect)
Members identify with the ingroup and conform
The group takes a more extreme decision

games.title: Concept and meaning

quiz.q: Group polarisation refers to:
options: Groups always choosing the middle path
The tendency of groups to make more extreme decisions than individuals alone
quiz.explain: Discussion strengthens the group's initial position.
steps: Group polarisation = groups making more extreme decisions than individuals alone.
The initial position grows stronger after discussion.
Answer: The tendency of groups to make more extreme decisions than individuals alone
quiz.mistake: Thinks groups always moderate views.

quiz.q: Which is a reason for group polarisation?
options: Hearing new arguments that favour one's own viewpoint
quiz.explain: Like-minded discussion offers more supporting arguments.
steps: Like-minded discussion gives new arguments for one's own view.
That strengthens the position.
Answer: Hearing new arguments that favour one's own viewpoint
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with social loafing remedies.

quiz.q: Feeling that one's view is validated because many others share it is called the:
quiz.explain: The bandwagon effect strengthens views when others agree.
steps: Feeling validated because many share one's view.
That is the bandwagon effect.
Answer: Bandwagon effect
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the halo effect.

quiz.q: Groupthink was described by:
quiz.explain: Janis described groupthink.
steps: Groupthink was described by Irving Janis.
Answer: Irving Janis
quiz.mistake: Credits another social psychologist.

quiz.q: A key feature of groupthink is:
options: An illusion of unanimity that suppresses dissent
quiz.explain: Groupthink involves pressure for agreement and the illusion that all agree.
steps: Groupthink shows an illusion of unanimity, self-censorship and pressure on dissenters.
Answer: An illusion of unanimity that suppresses dissent
quiz.mistake: Describes good decision-making instead.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Members of a like-minded group often adopt more extreme positions after discussion.
Reason (R): When people perceive like-minded others as their ingroup, they identify with it and conform to its views.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; ingroup identification and conformity explain the stronger, more extreme positions.
steps: A: like-minded groups take more extreme positions – true.
R: members identify with the ingroup and conform – true.
Ingroup identification explains the shift.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link ingroup identification with polarisation.

quiz.q: Which step would best protect a committee against groupthink?
options: Assigning a member to argue the opposite view as devil's advocate
quiz.explain: A devil's advocate encourages critical evaluation.
steps: A devil's advocate argues the opposite view.
This encourages critical evaluation and protects against groupthink.
Answer: Assigning a member to argue the opposite view as devil's advocate
quiz.mistake: Picks a step that strengthens groupthink.

quiz.q: Case: Members of a startup team each feel moderately confident about expanding to five cities. After an excited meeting where everyone agrees, they decide to launch in 20 cities next month. This illustrates:
quiz.explain: The group's decision became more extreme than individual views — group polarisation.
steps: Moderate individual confidence (5 cities) turned into 20 cities after agreeing.
The decision became more extreme: group polarisation.
Answer: Group polarisation
quiz.mistake: Confuses extreme decisions with reduced effort.

teach.ask: Gappu worries: 'Our flock all slightly wanted to fly south. After chatting, we decided to fly to Antarctica! What happened?'
teach.praise: Eek! That's group polarisation — new arguments, bandwagon effect and ingroup identity pushed us to extremes!
teach.nudge: Can you name one reason why groups become more extreme?

revise.summary: Group polarisation is the tendency of groups to make more extreme decisions than individuals, due to new supporting arguments, the bandwagon effect and ingroup identification. Groupthink (Janis) is the cohesive group's drive for consensus over realistic judgement.
focus: The three reasons for group polarisation
Ways to prevent poor group decisions
remember: Group polarisation: initial position becomes stronger after discussion
Bandwagon effect: view validated because others share it
Groupthink: Irving Janis; illusion of unanimity, self-censorship
traps: Polarisation pushes groups to extremes, not to the middle
Groupthink involves suppressing, not encouraging, dissent
Don't confuse group polarisation with social loafing
